problem: Adversarial attacks were studied only on static 2D images or static 3D scenes. It is unclear whether they transfer to embodied agents (EQA, EVR) that navigate a dynamic environment and decide from a history of views.
motivation: Embodied agents observe objects from many views over a trajectory and use contextual objects to answer questions, so single-view or single-object attacks are likely weak. Studying attacks on the embodiment exposes blind spots, security risks, and gaps between agent perception and human perception.
key_idea: Generate 3D adversarial texture (or shape) perturbations on multiple contextual objects, chosen through a Grad-CAM-style trajectory attention module over historical views and optimized through a neural renderer.
insight: Perturbing several contextual objects within the top-K attended views beats static 3D attacks (MeshAdv, Zeng et al.) by a large margin. In the ablation over M, attack success rises until about 5 objects, and context helps most on location and composition questions (4.67% and 28.51% gains) but little on color questions, where agents focus on the target object. Perturbations also generalize across questions and start points, and transfer to other agents and to a black-box renderer with reduced strength.
method: Trajectory attention module: computes Grad-CAM-style gradient weights of P(y|H) w.r.t. feature maps for each of the last N views, applies ReLU and normalization, and selects the top K=3 most important views.

Spatially contextual perturbation: perturbs the physical parameters (texture, shape) of all M objects visible in the K selected views. The gradient update is weighted by the view attention weights and by an indicator of whether the object appears in each view.
Differentiable rendering: replaces the non-differentiable OpenGL renderer with a neural renderer (Kato et al.) so gradients flow end-to-end from the agent's loss to 3D object parameters.

Attack loss: minimizes P(y|S, R(X,c)) plus a λ-weighted perceptual loss, computed as the L2 distance between rendered clean and adversarial images. The constraint is 32/255 RGB change in rendered 2D space, with λ=1.
Expectation over transformations: optimizes over five views one meter from each object with azimuth uniform in 0–180°.
Optimization: SGD with momentum 0.9 and up to 60 iterations. The default attack is texture-only. Navigation attacks force a premature Stop prediction.

setting.backbone: Attack targets PACMAN-RL+Q, NAV-GRU, NAV-React, VIS-VGG (EQA), Embodied Mask R-CNN (EVR); the attacker is gradient-based optimization with a neural renderer
setting.training_data: Attack is per-scene optimization on EQA-v1 (648 train / 68 val / 58 test environments, 933 test questions). Agents are pretrained EQA baselines. Adversarial training experiments retrain PACMAN for 300 epochs.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB frames (224×224) plus question text
setting.action_space: EQA agent: forward / turn / stop, via planner-controller
setting.privileged: White-box access to agent gradients and 3D scene meshes and textures; black-box transfer to the original renderer

numbers.extra: Attack lowers performance, so lower accuracy is better. Texture perturbation bounded at 32/255 per frame. T-10 / T-30 / T-50 are reported in that order.
numbers.evidence: Table 1, PACMAN Ours row; clean PACMAN accuracy is 50.23/44.19/39.94

numbers_note: EVR accuracy is given only in text (89.91% to 18.32% under attack). Black-box renderer transfer results are only in figures. Adversarial training results (Table 3) are on a 110-question, 5-house test set.
results: Attack drops PACMAN QA accuracy from 50.23/44.19/39.94% to 6.17/4.26/3.42% (T-10/30/50) and EVR accuracy from 89.91% to 18.32%. It beats MeshAdv and Zeng et al., which reach about 13–17% accuracy, and also raises dT and dmin on navigation. Attacks transfer to other agents, generalize across questions and start points (accuracy stays under 10.2%), and partly transfer to a black-box renderer.
limitations: Evaluated only in the simulated EQA-v1 (House3D), with no physical-world attack. Transfer to a non-differentiable renderer is weaker.
Requires white-box gradients and access to the 3D scene, and the attack is optimized per scene and trajectory.
Adversarial training gives only partial robustness; adversarial QA accuracy stays at 23.56%.
